messages.subject: Reliability questions on CFA
messages.body_plain:
I'm running a single-factor CFA and am exploring the different options to calculate reliability. All 22 indicator variables are dichotomous (0/1), and I'm using the ordered statement to use WLSV for estimation. The fit stats support a single factor.

First, I used Cronbach's alpha (equivalent to KR-20, for dichotomous variables), from the psych package:
cronbach.alpha(dt)

This gave me an estimate of 0.778
I then used the reliability function in semTools:
reliability(dt_fit)
and got alpha=0.8894284

>From the help file for semTools, alpha is Cronbach's alpha. The notes in the output said it used polychoric correlation, not Pearson's, that's the only difference I can find. Would that account for a 0.1 difference, which seems like quite a bit? To make sure something wasn't wrong with cronbach.alpha, I ran the same data through Stata and got the same result. Any thoughts on this much appreciated.

A second type of reliability I ran was composite reliability (Fornell and Larcker, 1981), which is basically the square of the sum of the loadings, divided by the square of sum of loadings plus sum of error variance:
l<-inspect(dt_fit,"coef")$lambda
v<-diag(inspect(dt_fit,"coef")$theta)
cr<-sum(l)^2/(sum(l)^2+sum(v))

This results in 0.96.

Again, this is a big wow for me. I would expect Cronbach's alpha to underestimate reliability, since my loadings do not allow for essential tau-equivalence. But I did not expect a bump from 0.78 to 0.96.

Does this seem like a reasonable finding? Am I missing something here?

Any thoughts much appreciated.

Robin

messages.subject: Re: Help about CFA analysis
messages.body_plain:
The minimum function test stat indicates that the model does not fit perfectly, but that is not a very informative test because we shouldn't expect approximate models to reproduce data exactly unless the model is just-identified (with zero degrees of freedom).

The RMSEA indicates mediocre fit, and the CFI/TLI indicate good fit, at leaste using the DWLS estimator.  They indicate poor fit using the Robust estimator, but that is only because the baseline model fits so much better using the Robust estimator than the DWLS (I'm not sure why that would be the case).

If you are looking for more detailed clues as to how your model might be fitting the data, you should inspect your parameter estimates (e.g., Are the factor loadings high enough to support your contention that there is a common factor(s) underlying the indicators?).

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Error
messages.body_plain:
First, I notice that you are freeing the first factor loading by placing NA in front of it.  This is not necessary, but what is necessary is that you identify the model by fixing the factor variance to 1.  You can just use the lavaan argument "std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE" to standardize your latent variable(s), which automatically allows the first factor loadings to be freely estimated.

Regarding your use of the WLS.V argument, it doesn't sound like you want to use that.  The WLS.V argument allows you to weight the matrix of parameters being estimated, not the raw data matrix (i.e., "each individual has weight associated" doesn't sound like you are trying to weight the parameter matrix).  See the ?lavaan help page for details:
WLS.V  --  A user provided weight matrix to be used by estimator "WLS"; if the estimator is "DWLS", only the diagonal of this matrix will be used. For a multiple group analysis, a list with a weight matrix for each group. The elements of the weight matrix should be in the following order (if all data is continuous): first the means (if a meanstructure is involved), then the lower triangular elements of the covariance matrix including the diagonal, ordered column by column. In the categorical case: first the thresholds (including the means for continuous variables), then the slopes (if any), the variances of continuous variables (if any), and finally the lower triangular elements of the correlation/covariance matrix excluding the diagonal, ordered column by column.
I haven't used the "lavaan.survey" package before, but I understand that it is designed to allow researchers to incorporate sampling weights into their lavaan analyses, so you might want to look into that.

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lavaan.survey/index.html

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Testing mediation
messages.body_plain:
> I need still to calculate the indirect effect and the confidence interval.
> Can anyone help me to write a correct syntax?

Hello Bert,

The special operator := allows you to define new parameters from old ones, using labels.  For example, one of your indirect effects appears to be from GROEPEN --> COMPETENCE  --> ENGAGEMENT.  You can add labels to the individual regression parameters, then define the indirect effects, like so:

ENGAGEMENT ~ AUTONOMY + Beta1*COMPETENCE + RELATEDNESS + CONNECTING + APPRECIATION + GROEPEN
COMPETENCE ~ APPRECIATION + CONNECTING + Beta2*GROEPEN

Ind1 := Beta1 * Beta2

You can extend this by adding labels to all your parameters, and calculating whichever indirect effects you want to test.  You can even use :=  to define total effects from multiple indirect effects (e.g., totalInd := ind1 + ind2).

Make sure to use bootstrapping to calculate your SEs and 95% CIs for these parameters by adding these arguments to the sem() command:

fit <- sem(model1, data= y, se = "boot", bootstrap = 500)
parameterEstimates(fit, boot.ci.type = "perc")

You want to interpret significance tests of the raw parameter estimates, but the standardized estimates can be interpreted for effect size, etc.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Reliability questions on CFA
messages.body_plain:
>From the source code, I don't see an obvious difference in the way alpha is calculated in either package's function:

from {psych}
alpha.raw <- (1 - tr(C)/sum(C)) * (n/(n - 1))
from {semTools}
alpha[j] <- length(index)/(length(index) - 1) * (1 - sum(diag(sigma)) / sum(sigma))
-- replace C with sigma and n with length(index), and the tr(x) function is equivalent to sum(diag(x)).

But I wouldn't use either one of them.  Like you said, your indicators are not tau-equivalent (a rarely tenable assumption).  Does the value of omega differ between the two packages as well?

The jump in reliability between alpha and CR looks large, but not necessarily surprising.  There is another similar reliability measure calculated from factor loadings called Average Variance Extracted, in which you simply square your factor loadings before taking the sum (a sum of squares, not a squared sum):

CR <- sum(l)^2 / (sum(l)^2 + sum(v))
AVE <- sum(l^2) / (sum(l^2) + sum(v))

Notice that these values also differ, but one is not more right than the other.  These reliability estimates are all measures of the same concept, but they are not estimates of a single common value you would find in the population (i.e., AVE and CR would usually differ in the population, and both would differ from Omega).  Excluding alpha, if all these reliability measures (omega, CR, and AVE) indicate high reliability, then that's a consistent indication of high reliability using different quantifications of a common concept, and that's all I would expect that you need to report.

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Testing mediation
messages.body_plain:
> I think I overlook something, where can I find the CI’s?

When you run parameterEstimates(fit), the confidence interval (lower and upper limits, respectively) is the the last two columns.  As long as you include the se = "boot" argument in your call to lavaan() or sem(), then your call to parameterEstimates(fit) or summary(fit) will print the bootstrapped SEs for significance tests.  But I still prefer to use the bootstrapped CI for significance testing (i.e., does the interval contain 0 or some other null-hypothesized value?) because those are not necessarily symmetric around the point estimate, making them more appropriate for testing parameters you would not expect to be normally distributed, such as variances (or residual (co)variances).

Terry

messages.subject: Re: Reliability questions on CFA
messages.body_plain:
When data consist of categorical variables, Pearson's correlations are the correlation of the observed scores. Polychoric correlations are the correlation of the latent multivariate normal distribution underlying categorical variables. Polychoric correlations always have better values. This is why when we run continuous CFA and CFA for categorical variables on categorical data, the factor loadings in CFA with categorical data are higher. If you believe that your items have underlying latent multivariate normal distribution, polychoric correlation and categorical CFA is recommended.

I agree with Terry that if your scales are not tau-equivalent, coefficient alpha is not recommended. Coefficient alpha is the lower bound of population reliability. The estimate of population reliability is the coefficient omega.

Best,
Sunthud

On Fri, Aug 2, 2013 at 6:01 AM, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> From the source code, I don't see an obvious difference in the way alpha is calculated in either package's function:
>
> from {psych}
> alpha.raw <- (1 - tr(C)/sum(C)) * (n/(n - 1))
> from {semTools}
> alpha[j] <- length(index)/(length(index) - 1) * (1 - sum(diag(sigma)) / sum(sigma))
> -- replace C with sigma and n with length(index), and the tr(x) function is equivalent to sum(diag(x)).
>
> But I wouldn't use either one of them.  Like you said, your indicators are not tau-equivalent (a rarely tenable assumption).  Does the value of omega differ between the two packages as well?
>
> The jump in reliability between alpha and CR looks large, but not necessarily surprising.  There is another similar reliability measure calculated from factor loadings called Average Variance Extracted, in which you simply square your factor loadings before taking the sum (a sum of squares, not a squared sum):
>
> CR <- sum(l)^2 / (sum(l)^2 + sum(v))
> AVE <- sum(l^2) / (sum(l^2) + sum(v))
>
> Notice that these values also differ, but one is not more right than the other.  These reliability estimates are all measures of the same concept, but they are not estimates of a single common value you would find in the population (i.e., AVE and CR would usually differ in the population, and both would differ from Omega).  Excluding alpha, if all these reliability measures (omega, CR, and AVE) indicate high reliability, then that's a consistent indication of high reliability using different quantifications of a common concept, and that's all I would expect that you need to report.
>
> Terry

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Terry and Sunthud -

Those were my thoughts precisely. One question - I've run semTools omega (using the reliability function) and the omega function from the psych package. They do not come out the same.

semTools gives me

Omega Hierarchical:    0.78

I understand fully the semTools documentation on how Omega is calculated in that package, but the psych documentation is a little dense for me, though I understand more or less what it is doing. Thanks for any guidance you may be able to provide, I know this is a Lavaan forum and I don't want to get super off-topic.

Robin

On Sunday, August 4, 2013 2:01:24 AM UTC-4, Sunthud Pornprasertmanit wrote:
> When data consist of categorical variables, Pearson's correlations are the correlation of the observed scores. Polychoric correlations are the correlation of the latent multivariate normal distribution underlying categorical variables. Polychoric correlations always have better values. This is why when we run continuous CFA and CFA for categorical variables on categorical data, the factor loadings in CFA with categorical data are higher. If you believe that your items have underlying latent multivariate normal distribution, polychoric correlation and categorical CFA is recommended.
>
> I agree with Terry that if your scales are not tau-equivalent, coefficient alpha is not recommended. Coefficient alpha is the lower bound of population reliability. The estimate of population reliability is the coefficient omega.
>
> Best,
> Sunthud
>
>
> On Fri, Aug 2, 2013 at 6:01 AM, Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > From the source code, I don't see an obvious difference in the way alpha is calculated in either package's function:
> >
> > from {psych}
> > alpha.raw <- (1 - tr(C)/sum(C)) * (n/(n - 1))
> > from {semTools}
> > alpha[j] <- length(index)/(length(index) - 1) * (1 - sum(diag(sigma)) / sum(sigma))
> > -- replace C with sigma and n with length(index), and the tr(x) function is equivalent to sum(diag(x)).
> >
> > But I wouldn't use either one of them.  Like you said, your indicators are not tau-equivalent (a rarely tenable assumption).  Does the value of omega differ between the two packages as well?
> >
> > The jump in reliability between alpha and CR looks large, but not necessarily surprising.  There is another similar reliability measure calculated from factor loadings called Average Variance Extracted, in which you simply square your factor loadings before taking the sum (a sum of squares, not a squared sum):
> >
> > CR <- sum(l)^2 / (sum(l)^2 + sum(v))
> > AVE <- sum(l^2) / (sum(l^2) + sum(v))
> >
> > Notice that these values also differ, but one is not more right than the other.  These reliability estimates are all measures of the same concept, but they are not estimates of a single common value you would find in the population (i.e., AVE and CR would usually differ in the population, and both would differ from Omega).  Excluding alpha, if all these reliability measures (omega, CR, and AVE) indicate high reliability, then that's a consistent indication of high reliability using different quantifications of a common concept, and that's all I would expect that you need to report.

messages.subject: Re: Reliability questions on CFA
messages.body_plain:
I agree that users need to be careful. On one hand, the current practice of calculating alpha (or KR-20) is equivalent to the tau-equivalent model treating dichotomous variables as continuous variables. The normality assumption is violated. On the other hand, reliability is defined as the proportion of true score variance over observed score variance. Using polychoric correlation does not calculate totally based on "observed" score variance but "latent" score variance. Thus, I think both ways are not ideal solutions. If I have no choice, I may go conservative by using KR-20 (the current practice). Some guidelines are available for interpretation of the magnitude. I think the following article may provide the solution.

Raykov, T., Dimitrov, D. M., & Asparouhov, T. (2010). Evaluation of scale reliability with binary measures using latent variable modeling. Structural Equation Modeling, 17(2), 265-279.

Sunthud

On 08/22/2013 03:38 AM, oolve...@gmail.com wrote:

> mod1 <- y ~ 1*x1 + 1*x2
>

> datum <- simulateData(mod1, sample.nobs=100, skewness=c(-1,1,1),
> kurtosis=c(0,0,0))
>
> you *still* get
>
> Error in MASS::mvrnorm(n = n, mu = rep(0, nvar), Sigma = ICOR) :
>    'Sigma' is not positive definite

Hm. I think what happens here is that the residual variance of y (which
by default is 1.0) is too small (given the coefficients 1, and the
default variances of x1/x2, also 1). When we force negative skew, this
results in non-positive definite covariance matrix.

Either lowering the coefficients (say, 0.1), or increasing the residual
variance seem to work:

mod1 <- ' y ~ 1*x1 + 1*x2

           y ~~ 10*y '

datum <- simulateData(mod1, sample.nobs=100, skewness=c(-1,1,1),

                       kurtosis=c(0,0,0), debug=TRUE)

If you think of the coefficients as 'standardized', it is better to use
the standardized=TRUE argument. This would still fail, but give a
warning saying the coefficients are >= 1.

Yves.

There are a couple of options. The measurementInvariance function will return a list of lavaan objects (one for each model fit). For example if you ran the following code:

fit<-measurementInvariance(HW.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, group="school")

summary(fit[[3]]) #this is a summary of the strong invariance model
summary(fit[[4]]) #this is a summary of the mean invariant model

Alternatively you could use the group.equal option in any of the lavaan functions (cfa, sem, growth or lavaan) to accomplish the same thing.

Ah but using multiple imputations should matter! The issue with any sort of nested model test using imputed data is that we simply don't know what best practice is for testing differences. This is illustrated by the issue of assessing fit with multiply imputed data. With MI you can compute 3-4 different chi square statistics. Which of these performs best remains an open question for research. So which chi square to use for model difference testing also remains an open question. For that reason we haven't built an anova method for results that come from imputed data. In your case, I'd advice using FIML with auxiliary variables to test for measurement invariance.

Hope this helps,

messages.body_plain:
Ah yes. Within the summaries of individual models the latent means should be reported (look under the Intercepts section). Specifically if you save the results from measurementInvariance as an object the third element of that list (e.g. fit[[3]]) from above, contains the estimates of latent means (with the first group set to 0). Now by default lavaan will set the scale of the model by fixing the first factor loading to 1 and the means in the first group to 0. If you want to set the scale a different way, then the syntax gets a bit more complex.

I should also mention that the same results can be obtained by fitting models using the group.equal argument in any of the lavaan functions (cfa, sem, growth, lavaan). By setting group.equal = c("loadings", "intercepts") you will fit a strong invariant model.

Hope that helps.

Alex
